topic: Biology — Biodiversity and the effect of human interaction on ecosystems
subject: combined-science

items.q: What is meant by the biodiversity of an ecosystem?
items.correct: The variety of different species living there
items.misconception: The total number of organisms living there
items.why: Students meet population size and biodiversity in the same topic, and 'more living things' feels like 'more biodiversity'. Counting individuals is also the easier thing to do in a practical survey. Biodiversity is the variety of all the different species of organisms on earth, or within an ecosystem. It is judged by the variety of species present, not by the number of individuals.
items.random_wrong: Number of different habitats found in the area

items.q: A woodland has a great biodiversity. Why is this ecosystem more stable?
items.correct: Each species depends less on others for its food
items.misconception: The number of individual organisms stays the same
items.why: Students meet population size and biodiversity in the same topic, and 'more living things' feels like 'more biodiversity'. Counting individuals is also the easier thing to do in a practical survey. Biodiversity is the variety of all the different species of organisms on earth, or within an ecosystem. It is judged by the variety of species present, not by the number of individuals.
items.random_wrong: Each species depends more on others for shelter

items.q: As the human population grows, more untreated sewage and fertiliser drain into a river and many fish and plants die. What is the effect on the river?
items.correct: Pollution kills plants and animals so biodiversity falls
items.misconception: There is no pollution since both are natural
items.why: The word 'pollution' is popularly linked with chemical spills and factory smoke, and 'natural' is often treated as meaning harmless. Pollution can occur in water, from sewage, fertiliser or toxic chemicals; in air, from smoke and acidic gases; and on land, from landfill and from toxic chemicals. Pollution kills plants and animals which can reduce biodiversity.
items.random_wrong: Biodiversity is unchanged as fish numbers recover

items.q: Part of an area of grassland is quarried for stone and the rest is ploughed to grow crops. What is the effect on other animals and plants?
items.correct: Less land is left for other plants and animals
items.misconception: Quarrying reduces the land but farming does not
items.why: Farmland looks green and 'natural' compared with towns, so students do not picture it as land removed from other species, even though a crop field supports few species. Humans reduce the amount of land available for other animals and plants by building, quarrying, farming and dumping waste. All four activities take habitat away from other species.
items.random_wrong: Biodiversity is unchanged as many individuals stay

items.q: A peat bog is drained and the peat is dug out and sold as garden compost. What are the effects?
items.correct: The habitat is lost and carbon dioxide is released
items.misconception: Carbon dioxide is released only by burning
items.why: Combustion is the release process students meet most often, and decay is slow and invisible, so it is not recognised as a source of carbon dioxide. The decay or burning of the peat releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere. Peat spread on soil as compost decays, so carbon dioxide is still released.
items.random_wrong: Biodiversity is unchanged as many organisms survive

items.q: Levels of carbon dioxide and methane in the atmosphere are increasing. Which is a biological consequence of the global warming this causes?
items.correct: Some species change the areas in which they are found
items.misconception: Species die out where the air becomes warmer
items.why: Warming is understood as a temperature problem, so students think about heat directly killing organisms rather than about habitats being lost or species moving to areas that now suit them. Biological consequences of global warming include loss of habitat, changes in the distribution of species and changes in migration patterns, as well as effects on individual organisms.
items.random_wrong: Areas near carbon dioxide sources are affected most

items.q: A government wants to reduce the negative effects of humans on ecosystems and biodiversity. Which policy would have a positive impact?
items.correct: Reducing forest loss and carbon dioxide emissions
items.misconception: Growing more crops that will be used to make biofuels
items.why: Biofuels are presented as an environmentally friendly alternative to fossil fuels, so students assume every consequence of producing them must also be beneficial. Large-scale deforestation in tropical areas has occurred to provide land for cattle and rice fields and to grow crops for biofuels. Clearing the forest destroys habitats and reduces biodiversity, whatever the crop is used for.
items.random_wrong: Spreading extra fertiliser on farmland each season

items.q: A nature reserve contains woodland, grassland and a lake. Does this by itself tell you the reserve has a high biodiversity?
items.correct: No. Biodiversity depends on the variety of different species present, not on how many habitats the reserve contains.
items.misconception: Biodiversity means the number of different habitats or ecosystems in an area.
items.why: Habitats are the visible, easily counted feature of a site, and textbooks often illustrate biodiversity with pictures of contrasting habitats, so students transfer the word from species to places. Biodiversity is the variety of all the different species of organisms on earth, or within an ecosystem. A variety of habitats may support many species, but it is the variety of species that is measured.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why does a great biodiversity make an ecosystem more stable?
items.correct: Because it reduces the dependence of one species on another for food, shelter and the maintenance of the physical environment.
items.misconception: The more species there are, the more each species depends on the others, so a high biodiversity makes an ecosystem less stable and losing species makes it more stable.
items.why: Students learn that organisms in a food web are interdependent, and assume that more species must mean more links and therefore more risk, rather than more alternatives. A great biodiversity ensures the stability of ecosystems by reducing the dependence of one species on another for food, shelter and the maintenance of the physical environment. Losing species reduces stability.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which gases named in the specification are increasing in the atmosphere and contribute to global warming?
items.misconception: Carbon dioxide is the only gas that contributes to global warming; methane is a separate problem that does not affect it.
items.why: Carbon dioxide dominates news coverage and earlier topics on combustion and photosynthesis, so methane is remembered only as a product of decay or digestion. Levels of carbon dioxide and methane in the atmosphere are increasing, and both contribute to 'global warming'.
